lessons.gloss: please — literally "having done a kindness," and the noun-plus-করা pattern's third demonstration

segments.text: The heart word closed the last chapter. A new one opens on a feeling that starts in the same place — and a word this book has never taught you before now.

blocks.title: You'll want to know: দয়া করে

segments.text: দয়া করে — doya kore — please.
দয়া করে বসুন (doya kore bôshun) — please, sit.
দয়া is দ (dô) plus য় (the glide already met inside হৃদয়) with the vowel sign া (ā): doyā. করে is ক (kô) plus র (r) with the vowel sign ে (e): kôre.

দয়া is Sanskrit দয়া (dayā), "compassion, pity." Most Indo-Europeanists trace its root back to PIE deh₂-, "to divide, to apportion" — the same root proposed for Greek daíomai, "to divide," and dêmos, "a portion of land, the people," which English holds without inheriting it directly: democracy, epidemic, demographic. If the comparison is right, compassion and sharing are the same idea at the root — you feel দয়া for someone by dividing your own good fortune with them, the warmth this book already located in হৃদয়, the heart.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: করা wears a new outfit

segments.text: Noun plus করা already builds a verb — কাজ করা, "to work"; জিজ্ঞাসা করা, "to ask." Here করা takes a different shape, করে, "having done": not a full sentence on its own, but a piece that leans on the next word.

utterances: shape of করা: a finite ending (করি, করে, করেন…) job: states an action. example: আমি কাজ করি — I work.
shape of করা: করে, unchanged. job: "having done," leaning forward. example: দয়া করে (doya kore) বসুন — please, sit.

segments.text: দয়া করে (doya kore) literally says "having done a kindness, [now do this]" — the kindness is named, then the actual request follows.

segments.instruction: the family this word joins — "kāj kôrā … jijñāsā kôrā … doya kore"
segments.source: [YOU SAY: the family this word joins — "kāj kôrā … jijñāsā kôrā … doya kore"]

segments.text: What does দয়া করে (doya kore) mean literally, piece by piece? ("Having done a kindness" — দয়া "compassion" + করে "having done.") Is করে here a full sentence by itself? (No — it leans forward onto the request that follows it.) One quick reach back: what root does দয়া share with a very old disputed argument about democracy? (PIE deh₂-, "to divide" — the same proposed root behind Greek dêmos, and behind the warmth হৃদয়, the heart, already carries — two lessons after নাক, the nose, which shares none of it.)

lessons.title: দুঃখিত (dukkhito) — "sorry," and a prefix that reaches Greek
lessons.gloss: sorry — built on a word two dictionaries explain two different ways, and a prefix with a real Greek cousin

needs: your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your eyes, so it is not fully a driving lesson. You will want your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now — leave the section called The letters in this word until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: Last lesson's kindness gets a request said politely. This lesson is what you say when the kindness came too late.
দুঃখিত — dukkhito — sorry.
আমি দুঃখিত (āmi dukkhito) — I'm sorry.

দুঃখিত is দ (dô) with the vowel sign ু (u), then ঃ — a new mark, the visarga, two small stacked dots that add a light breath after the vowel — then খ (kh) with the vowel sign ি (i), then ত (t, silent at the end). Spelled duḥkhita, said dukkhito: the breath mark softens toward the consonant that follows it rather than staying a separate sound.

দুঃখিত (dukkhito) is built on Sanskrit দুঃখ (duḥkha), "sorrow, suffering" — the word Buddhism made famous as dukkha. Take it apart and one half is certain: দুঃ/দুস্ (dus-) means "bad, difficult," from PIE dus-, the very prefix inside Greek dys-: dystopia, dysfunctional. The other half, খ (kha), is where the certainty ends. Sanskrit's own grammatical tradition explains it as "an axle-hole" — a duḥkha journey is a bad axle-hole, a rough ride, set against সুখ (sukha), "a good axle-hole," comfort. It is a vivid story, and it is repeated everywhere. It is also, by the account of modern Sanskritists including Mayrhofer, not a story to trust: the axle-hole reading may be a later folk explanation grafted onto a word whose real root is lost. দুঃ's cousin is real; খ's is a story, reported and not settled.

segments.instruction: the secure half and its Greek cousin — "dus- … dystopia"

segments.instruction: last lesson's request again — "doya kore bôshun"

segments.text: Say "I'm sorry" in Bengali. (আমি দুঃখিত (dukkhito).) Which half of দুঃখ is a secure PIE prefix, and which English word shares it? (দুঃ/dus-, "bad" — dystopia, by way of Greek dys-.) Is the "bad axle-hole" story of খ settled fact? (No — a repeated tradition, treated with real skepticism by modern Sanskritists.) Sorrow, like compassion, can weigh somewhere specific — where? (হৃদয়, the heart.)

lessons.title: মাফ করবেন (maf korben) — "excuse me," borrowed and softened
lessons.gloss: excuse me — the same Persian loan Hindi's own "sorry" phrase uses, softened here by the future tense rather than a command

segments.text: Last lesson's word for "sorry" was a native Sanskrit word. This one is a loanword — the very same loanword Hindi uses in its own "sorry" phrase — and it softens a request in a way you have not met yet.

blocks.title: You'll want to know: মাফ করবেন

segments.text: মাফ করবেন — maf korben — excuse me.
মাফ করবেন, একটু জায়গা দেবেন? (maf korben, êktu jāygā debên?) — excuse me, could you make a little room?

মাফ is ম (mô) with া (ā) plus ফ (ph, the puffed p). Notice what is missing: Hindi marks this same borrowed sound with a small dot under its own letter for pha, a nuqtā, to write a dedicated letter for f. Bengali's script has no such mark at all — ফ alone serves for both the native puffed p and this borrowed f, and only habit tells a reader which one a given word means.

মাফ is not Bengali, and not Sanskrit: it is borrowed, by way of Persian, from Arabic 'afw, "to pardon, to wipe a wrong away." Hindi borrowed the identical word for the identical job. Bengali also keeps a formal, Sanskritic cousin for the same idea, ক্ষমা করবেন, from ক্ষমা (kṣamā), "patience, forbearance" — the everyday loan and the bookish native word side by side, the same split Hindi keeps.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: the future, asked to be gentle

segments.text: The tea-offering pattern you already own reuses a present verb — আপনি খান — to make a request. করবেন does the same job with a different tense: it is the plain future, "you will do," not a command at all by its grammar, and yet its job here is exactly a request — a third shape for করা, beside last lesson's participle করে.

utterances: tense used: present habitual. what it does: states, and doubles as a request. example: আপনি খান — you eat / please eat.
tense used: future. what it does: states, and doubles as a softer request. example: মাফ করবেন (maf korben) — you will excuse / please excuse.

segments.text: The future's distance is what buys the softness: asking rather than telling, even grammatically.

segments.instruction: the two soft requests compared — "chā khān … maf korben"
segments.source: [YOU SAY: the two soft requests compared — "chā khān … maf korben"]

segments.text: Where does মাফ come from? (Arabic 'afw, "to pardon," by way of Persian — the same loan Hindi's own "sorry" phrase uses.) What tense is করবেন, and why does that make it gentler than a command? (Future — "you will do," asking rather than telling.)

lessons.title: স্বাগতম (shbagotom) — "welcome," a good arrival
lessons.gloss: welcome — "a good coming," built on the same "hither" prefix already met, and a verb whose PIE root is unusually secure

needs: your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your eyes, so it is not fully a driving lesson. You will want your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now — leave the section called The letters in this word until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: This chapter has taught what to say after a mistake. It closes on what to say before anything goes wrong at all — a word built on the same "hither" you have carried since the verb for coming.
স্বাগতম — shbagotom — welcome.
আমাদের বাড়িতে স্বাগতম (āmāder bāṛite shbagotom) — welcome to our house.

স্বাগতম (shbagotom) is স্ব (a conjunct, স joined straight to ব with no vowel between — sbô, tilted by the same s becomes sh habit every Sanskrit word in this book has shown) plus া (ā), then গ (gô), ত (tô), and ম (mô, keeping its own inherent vowel at the very end): shbā-go-to-m.

স্বাগতম (shbagotom) is Sanskrit স্বাগতম (shbagotom) (svāgatam), built from two pieces fused together. The second piece, আগত (āgata), "arrived, come," opens with the very same আ-, "hither," that আসা's own lesson already named — except here it rides a different verb, √গম্ (√gam, "to go, to come"), not আসা's own unsettled stem. √gam is PIE gʷem-, and this root is about as secure as roots get: it is the direct ancestor of English come, and, by way of Latin venīre, of advent and convene too. The first piece, সু- (su-, "good"), loses its vowel to the glide ব when the next syllable also opens with a vowel — ordinary Sanskrit sandhi, the same trade সু- plus আগত makes every time: svāgata. সু- is PIE h₁su-, cousin of Greek eu-, the "good" inside eulogy and euphoria. Put the pieces back together: স্বাগতম (shbagotom) is, literally, "a good coming."

segments.text: Give "welcome" in Bengali. (স্বাগতম (shbagotom).) What does স্বাগতম (shbagotom) mean, piece by piece? ("Good" plus "come" — a good arrival.) Which prefix does it share with আসা, and on a different verb this time? (আ-, "hither" — on √gam here, not আসা's own uncertain stem.) Run this chapter's three other new words back: a kindness done, a word for sorrow, and a borrowed pardon. (দয়া করে (doya kore), দুঃখিত (dukkhito), মাফ করবেন (maf korben).) One more reach: what tense softened that pardon into a request? (Future — করবেন, "you will do.")
